https://habr.com/ru/articles/1077976/?ut.summary: For over a year and a half, I've been building a digital twin: a knowledge base containing my life's data from the past decade, and an agent that uses this base. I started like everyone else, with Obsidian and Claude. My first conclusions came after uploading 219,353 files. For me, Obsidian is now just a viewer, not what I initially thought. The value of this data lies in three things: plain text files on disk, links and interconnections between them, and an agent that reads and writes them directly. This article explains how it's set up now and how many tokens have been spent. My goal was to create a digital twin – a system that thinks and responds like me, remembers everything I remember, and even what I've forgotten. This requires a properly functioning memory, not a vector database with 500-token blocks, but a structured one with history. I installed Obsidian, created a vault, and started dumping notes, documents, and stories – everything. I expected Obsidian to be the home of my memory, the graph to be a functional tool for finding forgotten information, not just a visual, and plugins to cover all my needs: linking notes, creating tables, and connecting to a neural network. I also expected seamless synchronization and for the agent to work with the base through it. Only the graph's aesthetics and the readability of notes met these expectations. Obsidian is not a knowledge base; for me, it's a viewer for a folder of text files. It's beautiful, with a graph and plugins. The agent doesn't need Obsidian at all. Claude Code reads and writes files directly, without bridge plugins or intermediaries. Synchronization also bypasses Obsidian's cloud. Syncthing works well; I have six machines, each with a full data copy. I'm keeping Obsidian for its graph visualization and note readability, but its role is far from what I imagined from reviews and descriptions. Perhaps my initial mistake was (and many make it) dumping everything into text files: chat logs, dumps. The vault grew rapidly, search worsened, and token usage increased due to sifting through irrelevant information. My current data storage and processing are structured in three layers. Layer 1: Facts. Raw data in SQLite databases (Telegram archive, browser history, counters). Questions of 'how much,' 'when,' and 'who' are resolved by database queries, costing zero tokens. Layer 2: Meaning. After selecting notes, I perform value-based search on my GPU, saving tokens. The agent queries it and receives the five closest notes for reading. Layer 3: Thoughts. The AI and I write summaries: decisions, rules, profiles, analyses. Raw information doesn't enter the vault. I use inexpensive tools first: database queries and file searches are free. Value-based search is cheap. The AI model is called last, only when its judgment is needed, and it receives pre-selected information. A mandatory rule: the agent must always retrieve context before starting work. For example, when writing an email, the agent reads the recipient's card, correspondence history, and past interactions. When starting a task, it checks if it's been done before. At the start of a session, it runs the query through search and works based on the input. Second rule: everything processed by the agent is saved. Each saved file undergoes four steps: the original is preserved, a note with a description and source is saved, the search is re-indexed, and links to neighboring notes are added. The note header includes title, date, type, source, machine, and tags. The 'machine' field is crucial as six machines and multiple people write to the vault, aiding in quick orientation. The most useful outcome is my voice profile. A script analyzed all 958,014 of my messages over ten years, collecting statistics on greetings, filler words, introductions, sales pitches, and reminders. Now, when the agent writes as me, it consults this profile to mimic my style. Messages after 2025 were counted separately as AI writing quality varied. Figures: 219,353 text files, 280 concepts (graph core), 5.9 GB Telegram archive (958,014 messages), 6 machines synced via Syncthing, value-based search on GPU. Challenges: Syncthing conflicts with multiple machines writing to one folder (mitigated by 'one file, one writer' rule and conflict monitoring script). Incorrect conclusions due to robots not finding information (now agent searches all locations before concluding absence). High cost of loading files per session (mitigated by measuring token cost of new rules and nightly compression). My logic: raw data to database, meaning to search, thoughts to text files. Violating this costs money. In the end: after 1.5 years, I have a vendor-independent memory: disk files, SQLite, open Syncthing. Obsidian and Claude can be replaced, but the files remain. The agent wakes up knowing the context: decisions made, promises given, yesterday's issues. Everything described is on my GitHub. Feel free to ask questions; I'm happy to share my 1.5 years of setup and reconfiguration.
https://habr.com/ru/articles/1077976/?ut.title: I Reconsidered My Stance on Obsidian After Building a Second Brain with 219,000 Files

https://habr.com/ru/articles/1082236/?ut.summary: Internal models of frontier labs are not publicly available. I don't really believe in conspiracy theories like "OpenAI has a real AGI in its basement and is only releasing a cut-down ChatGPT." The model used by its own researchers and the model sold through the API don't have to be the same. Frontier labs create not one neural network, but a factory of models: research checkpoints > experimental models > reward models > teacher models > models for generating synthetic data > model evaluators > distilled students > production models, and only the last element of the chain reaches the public. Why distillation is needed Suppose you've trained a monstrously expensive model that reasons well, writes code, and solves math problems, but each query to it costs enormous computational resources. For an in-house researcher, it's a working tool, and it's worth it if trillion-dollar markets are at stake. For a product with 100 million users, scaling access to such models is profitable, so instead of running it for every query, it's made into a teacher: it generates high-quality answers, solutions, reasoning trajectories, synthetic data, sometimes probability distributions themselves, and a smaller student is trained on this behavior, which doesn't need to reproduce the teacher entirely, but only transfer the necessary capabilities. This is one form of knowledge distillation, and the practice is so common that OpenAI directly provides developers with an official Model Distillation workflow: take answers from a stronger model, like GPT-4o or o1-preview, and train a cheaper model on them. OpenAI's own wording is quite precise: take an advanced model and achieve comparable quality on a specific task at a significantly lower cost. From this follows a rather simple thing: the best research model and the best production model are optimized for different functions, because the research model maximizes capabilities, while the production model has to simultaneously balance intelligence, latency, GPU cost, throughput, reliability, and safety. https://habr.com/ru/articles/1083130/?ut.summary: Reflections on a project. Architecture: router + pipelines (AWS, Claude). We'll consider a relatively simple example familiar to almost everyone who has built an LLM agent for natural language queries to data – whether it's text2sql, an analytical assistant, or a database chatbot. Typically, the agent is tasked with handling everything itself – determining the query type, formulating it, choosing the output format, and deciding whether to issue a disclaimer. This is the essence of an agent and the purpose of the system prompt. The system works flawlessly for a dozen test questions. But problems arise later when questions start coming in different formulations. For example, the same question phrased differently is processed differently – the model interprets the phrase differently, and structurally identical results take on different forms (string, table, graph) without explanation. Or, for the same question phrasing, a disclaimer is sometimes provided and sometimes comes back empty. The first thing usually changed in such cases is adding another rule to the prompt. This helps a few times. Then the new rule contradicts the old ones, and the prompt becomes a collection of patches for specific situations. The instability doesn't disappear; it just hides in the order in which the model applies conflicting instructions. This is where both the problem and its solution lie. The problem is that in the described scenario, no one explicitly decided what part of the system is handled by code and what by the model. It evolved organically during prompt generation. If you ask why the model chooses the output format instead of a developer writing ten lines of ordinary code, there's usually no clear answer. Hence the solution: the boundary between what the code does and what the model does is not an implementation detail but a separate architectural object. If this decision isn't made explicitly, it will still be made by default, and most often not in favor of system stability. Read more
https://habr.com/ru/articles/1083130/?ut.title: The Code | Model Boundary as an Architectural Object

https://habr.com/ru/articles/1083156/?ut.summary: An analyst at a webinar asked about hierarchical indexes for regulatory documents: a tree of 'document → article → clause', where the model descends from the root and selects a branch, like a person browsing a table of contents. Then, about costs: indexing involves processing the entire corpus. I compared such an index to a B-tree. Then I sat down to calculate, and the comparison held up. In a B-tree on disk, a node is fitted to a block to reduce head movements. Here, the block is the effective window of a small model, and head movement is a call to it. Let's estimate. Six acts of ~200 pages — depth 2. 2M tokens — depth 3. The navigator reads 8–12 thousand tokens instead of the entire corpus. And the tree itself already exists in the laws: chapters, articles, parts, clauses. It's built with regexps based on numbering, without a model. Costs are one-time, only for a brief description of internal nodes. The navigator only needs to choose one of fifty branches based on a short description. This is closer to classification than reasoning. Someone in the audience asked if a 1.5–3 billion parameter model could handle this. Intriguing. In this article, we'll explore ways to get accurate answers from legally significant documentation. Read more

https://habr.com/ru/articles/1084140/?ut.summary: I ran 20 prompts through the Perplexity API three times each, collected 60 answers, and for each citation [N] in the text, I linked the answer sentence to the source page it points to. Then came the most labor-intensive part: for each such pair—answer sentence and source page—I searched the HTML for a text snippet that most closely matched the statement in the answer. Out of 1355 citations, 948 led to pages that were still accessible, and on 448 of them, I found a passage—a paragraph, list item, or table cell—covering at least a third of the words in the statement. https://habr.com/ru/articles/1085652/?ut.summary: Over the past few years, the wrapper around LLM models has evolved from a simple chat interface and a rules file in an editor to a self-sufficient technological layer – the harness – with its own protocols, standards, and foundation. Client lock-in has shifted from the specific LLM model level to this harness level. Definitions: 1. Model – an LLM, a neural network that generates text on demand. It is stateless (doesn't remember previous calls), has no access to the external world, and is incapable of action – only generating the next token or a probable set of phrases based on the input context. 2. Harness – the software and infrastructure wrapper around the model, transforming it from a text generator into a system capable of performing "meaningful" actions. The harness provides the model with functionality: tools (access to the external world), context management (memory, sessions, compaction), rules/instructions (behavior), permissions and rights (security), and optionally enhancements – hooks, skills, orchestration. The harness is the "body," the model is the "semantic brain." 3. AI Agent – a model placed within a harness, thus capable of acting, i.e., perceiving the environment's state through tools, maintaining context between steps, planning, and executing multi-step tasks. An agent is not a component but the result of combining a model and a harness. Below is an approximate account of the development of harness ideas and its current state. Read more

https://habr.com/ru/articles/1087018/?ut.summary: Not the history of all human inventions, but a single conditional trajectory: how the Western scientific and technical system repeatedly expanded the space of subsequent possible solutions. If we look at human history on a cosmic scale, the difference between a person who simply wanted to stay warm by the fire and an engineer at a nuclear power plant seems almost like the blink of an eye. If we exaggerate this image to a joke, it becomes extremely rapid: a hypothetical Cro-Magnon is still thinking about how to get warm, and in a historical instant, his descendants already have a nuclear power plant running. Of course, tens of thousands of years, a huge number of cultures, wars, migrations, discoveries, and vanished branches lie between these points. But the contrast itself is useful: biologically, humans have not turned into a different species during this time, while the external machine for knowledge production has grown enormously. It is this external machine that interests me in this article. I am not trying to retell the history of human inventions, nor am I proposing a universal periodization of civilizations. There will be no separate study of Ancient Egypt, Greece, Rome, China, India, or other great scientific traditions, although their contribution is enormous and many of their achievements have entered the European lineage. For our task, it is sufficient to consciously narrow the field and look at one realized trajectory – the one that, from the late Middle Ages onwards, gradually formed the modern Western and North Atlantic scientific and technical world. Such a limitation is not a statement about the superiority of this trajectory, nor an attempt to declare it the only viable one. It is a research perspective. In the book "The Firm's Brain: 2026," viability is considered not as a single predetermined route, but as a field of continuations: it is important not only what option exists now, but also what possibilities it leaves behind, how independent they are, and how much it costs to keep them open. I am transferring this idea to history solely as a way of posing the question: which institutions, technologies, and ways of organizing knowledge not only yielded immediate results but also expanded the field of subsequent results? https://habr.com/ru/articles/1089742/?ut.summary: Our AI orchestrator has over ninety tools: working with tables, documents, email, tasks, web pages, presentations, etc. When processing requests, the model chooses which one to call at each step. The question that periodically arises is: how many of them should it be shown at once – all, or only those relevant to the request? Our orchestrator can work with both large cloud models and small ones that fit on a consumer graphics card. The minimum working configuration: RTX 3090 24Gb + Qwen3.6 27B. The goal is to make the minimum working configuration perform corporate tasks with acceptable quality and speed. Clearly, the method of selecting tools should differ for small and large models, but finding the optimal option is a complex question. Usually, the orchestrator shows the model the entire list of tools, and it decides which one to choose to answer the request. Hermes, OpenClaw, and Ouroboros do this. None of them select tools based on the request text. Some have a mode for weak models and small contexts where models are given only a catalog – name and short description – and the tool to "connect", so it finds and loads the necessary one itself. These agents are designed for frontier models like Claude and GPT-5, which can handle a hundred tools without loss. My task is different: to work on a local 27B in a closed environment. For it, a narrow set is measurably better. How a narrow set is structured The scheme is simple. Before the main model call, a router works: based on the request text, it selects a section – "datasets", "email", "presentations"... – and a subsection within the section. The model receives not ninety, but about twenty tool descriptions. It is unaware of the existence of the others at this stage. Read more

https://habr.com/ru/articles/1090426/?ut.summary: In May, I submitted OenoBench, a wine benchmark for language models, to NeurIPS. During discussions with reviewers, a question arose that neither I nor they had a basis for: what result at release is sufficient for a new benchmark, and how long will it last? To answer this, I collected data on 224 benchmarks reported between 2018 and 2026 by nine labs: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI, DeepSeek, Alibaba, Moonshot, and Mistral. For each, I found its birth date and, if it had passed, its death date—the moment the benchmark can no longer distinguish top models: the leader achieves 90% or human-level performance, or the creators themselves declare the set saturated or broken. From these dates, I calculated the half-life: the time it takes for half of the benchmarks to die. Key findings: The benchmark half-life is 23 months. For those released before 2023, it was 38 months; for those released later, it's 19 months. The estimate accounts for benchmarks still alive, so the short history of new ones doesn't distort it. New benchmarks are not easier than old ones; models are simply faster. The initial gap to the ceiling is the same, but models cross it twice as fast. Every seventh new benchmark dies not because of models, but due to its own defects. For agentic environments, this is the cause of nearly half of all deaths. Below is how I calculated this and how long, based on this data, OenoBench itself will last. The dataset, codebook, and scripts are publicly available, with links at the end. Read more

I recall, according to legend, the Rothschilds were the first to receive news of world events (especially military actions) and could take action for personal gain before others. But it wasn't just about reacting to events. Soon, people learned not only to transmit data quickly but also to control which data should be disseminated. This is called propaganda. Propaganda can be called an integral part of civilization. It is a common phenomenon that has existed for thousands of years. Remember Sparta and Athens? This is just another way to control information for the benefit of a certain group of people. In search of truth, people came up with a standard countermeasure against propaganda - expert opinion. However, it turned out that this opinion could also be controlled, even for money. And the question of finding the truth arose again. Then honor came onto the scene. A person who respects himself and is respected in society will not lie. And the longer a person is respected, as people have devised, the more valuable his word is. By the way, the methodology is also ancient, rooted in the prophets. https://habr.com/ru/articles/1096254/?ut.summary: For almost a year now, AI has been not an experiment for me, but a working tool: real projects, real deadlines, real responsibility for the result. And over this year, I've seen that people who "write code with AI" do it fundamentally differently. Some throw a prompt and take what comes out. Others design a system where AI does the work under their control. Andrey Karpaty, who coined the term "vibe coding" in February 2025, meant something simple: to whip up a business card website or a utility for oneself, without reading the code, trusting the result. But the word stuck to everything: from crafts to production systems where an engineer is responsible for every line. The difference between these two ways of working is huge, and a name for the second approach seems to be missing. On top of that, many truly abuse the technology and create quick, unverified solutions targeting responsible niches where they show their weakness, lack of refinement, and data security threats. Such solutions have added a negative connotation to the concept of "vibe coding," and real software engineers have inadvertently been lumped in with beginners and received the "shameful" label of vibe coder. This situation seemed unfair to me, not because engineers might be offended, but because there's a substitution of concepts, and a misconception on the business side when evaluating the product being created. Businesses in production don't need MVPs and "one-evening" crafts; they need an architecturally strong and reliable product for which the developer is responsible and provides guarantees. But suddenly, details emerge that were difficult to foresee: it turns out that before sending an order to the supervisor, an additional check is needed, and orders over 100,000 rubles must be confirmed by the director. From this, it's often concluded that vibe-coding cannot be used to build serious products. https://habr.com/ru/articles/1098436/?ut.summary: In one of the Ai2 Institute's tests, a language model was choosing an employee for an engineering position. The model compensated for missing certificates with reasoning about potential and diversity of experience. This example is from the FairStress research paper, published a few days ago. And it's unpleasant in its familiarity: the model adjusts its justification to its internal verdict, although the exact opposite is expected. https://habr.com/ru/companies/ostrovok/a.summary: The core of a basic agentic harness is a simple loop: an LLM receives a task, selects and calls a tool, the result is returned to the context, and then the model decides what action to take next. The loop continues until the model decides the task is complete. This loop is correct, but naive. One pilot in a good fighter jet can win a dogfight, but no one conducts an entire air operation like that. Real operations have mission planners who, even before takeoff, determine which sorties need to be flown; squadrons performing independent tasks in parallel; fuel limits and a bingo fuel signal after which you need to return to base; flight recorders that allow you to reconstruct the course of each sortie; and finally, post-mission debriefings to determine if the mission was truly successful. None of this replaces the pilot. All of this creates an infrastructure around them, thanks to which the system as a whole remains fast, safe, easy to debug, and measurable. The same happens with agents. In this article, we will take the basic agent loop and sequentially add typed tools, DAG and parallel execution, multi-level memory, verification, role separation of Planner / Worker / Critic, multi-dimensional budgets, and tracing – and then connect it all with a thin orchestrator. The entire experiment is built around one question: How to turn a simple agent loop into a reliable system capable of planning, acting, recovering from errors, and proving that it has done everything correctly? This publication is a translation and adaptation of Bruno Gonçalves' article Building an Advanced Agentic Harness, prepared by the Ostrovok team. In the original, the material continues the Data For Science series on the structure of agentic harnesses. Read more

The exercise is done, the box is ticked. The idea it was meant to convey often remains on the table with the broken spaghetti. We conduct research in the field of recommendations, develop new models, and, of course, compare our results with those of colleagues and other researchers. We regularly encounter situations where results claimed in a scientific paper or obtained from another team cannot be reproduced, even though the key parameters of the pipeline are identical. In this article, my colleague Anna Volodkevich and I will share our experience analyzing such discrepancies, which led us to develop the SplitLight framework. When the results of a scientific paper or the success of another team cannot be reproduced, people usually start by looking for bugs in the model implementation: they examine the architecture, loss function, and negative sampling method. While some discrepancies are indeed due to these factors, our practical experience shows that the data preparation procedure often has a greater impact on the final result of comparing recommender models. For example, the statement from a paper "Zvuk dataset, global temporal split with a quantile of 0.9" does not specify which filters and aggregations were applied, how events with identical timestamps and repeated interactions were handled, whether cold objects were removed, what data was fed to the model, and based on which events metrics were calculated. Therefore, two pipelines with the same dataset and the same split name might be evaluating different problem formulations. This hinders experiment reproducibility and comparison of results across works. Read more
